analysis.one_liner: Requires paper ballots for all federal elections and bans voting machines from connecting to the internet.
analysis.headline: The House passed the election security bill 225-184 in June 2019, but the Senate never voted on it, so no paper-ballot requirement became law.
analysis.plain_summary: The SAFE Act would have required every federal election to be cast on individual, durable, voter-verified paper ballots that can be counted by hand, with the paper ballot as the official record in any recount or audit. It would have required states to run statistical post-election audits of every federal race, banned voting systems from connecting to the internet or using wireless devices, required voting machines and ballots to be made in the United States, and required voting machine makers to publicly disclose their source code and hardware designs. It funded the transition with grants to states — $600 million for fiscal 2019 plus $175 million in several later years — and had the Election Assistance Commission test and decertify voting systems that fail cybersecurity guidelines.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, who would get a physical record of every vote they cast that they could inspect before it is counted and that could be recounted by hand without machines. Voters with disabilities, voters whose primary language is not English, and voters with literacy difficulties would benefit from NSF-funded research on accessible paper ballot verification. State and local election officials would receive federal grants to replace noncompliant machines, harden registration databases, and fund the mandatory audits.

how_it_helps.text: Every federal vote would be cast on a durable, voter-verified paper ballot that the voter can inspect before casting, and the paper ballot would be the official record for recounts and audits, with electronic tallies subordinate to it in a dispute.

States would have to conduct risk-limiting audits of every federal election — statistical checks with a 95 percent chance of correcting a wrong outcome — with the federal government covering the audit costs.

Voting systems could not be connected to the internet or use wireless communications, and tabulating devices would have to be built so they mechanically cannot change votes, with source code and hardware components disclosed for independent security review.
Voting machines would have to be manufactured in the United States and ballots printed on recycled American-made paper, and vendors would have to report cybersecurity incidents within three days.
The bill directed $600 million in fiscal 2019 and $175 million in each of fiscal 2020, 2022, 2024, and 2026 in grants to help states replace noncompliant systems and harden election infrastructure.

analysis.who_pays: Voting machine manufacturers would bear the largest cost: their proprietary business model would end, since they would have to publish source code and hardware designs under royalty-free licenses, stop connecting machines to networks, and build machines domestically. Federal taxpayers would fund the state grants and audit reimbursements. States would shoulder the administrative burden of new testing, reporting, and audit rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Voting machine vendors and federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The compliance timeline was tight: most new requirements applied to the 2020 election, and jurisdictions still using paper-record printers attached to electronic machines in 2018 got only a two-year delay, to 2022, which meant large replacement purchases on short notice.
Requiring every paper ballot in a recount or audit to be counted by hand is labor-intensive and would raise costs for local election offices, even with federal audit funding.

Requiring manufacturers to publicly disclose source code and hardware designs under royalty-free licenses, plus domestic-manufacture requirements, could reduce vendor participation or raise prices; the bill's own waiver process acknowledged some tabulation-device requirements might need temporary waivers.
The buy-American requirements for machines and recycled ballot paper could add costs for states, applying as early as January 2021 for ballot printing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — a verifiable paper record and mandatory audits for every federal election — addresses a real vulnerability, since many jurisdictions used paperless machines where a hack or error leaves no way to check the count. The costs are real but one-time and largely borne by vendors whose secrecy the bill targets, with federal grants cushioning states. The tight 2020 timeline and mandatory hand-counting for all recounts were legitimate design criticisms, but the bill's structure (grants, phased effective dates, waiver authority) tried to manage them.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on June 27, 2019, but the Senate referred it to its Rules Committee and never voted on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Zoe Lofgren introduced the SAFE Act in May 2019; it was referred to the House Administration and Science, Space, and Technology Committees.
The House Administration Committee reported the bill on June 26, 2019, by a 6-3 vote, and the Science Committee was discharged.

On June 27, 2019, Republicans moved to recommit the bill with instructions to require chief state election officials to disclose foreign nationals with access to ballots or voting machines; the motion failed 189-220, with 183 of 198 Republicans voting yes and all but 6 Democrats voting no.
The House passed the bill 225-184: 224 of 234 voting Democrats voted yes, while 184 of 198 voting Republicans voted no and only one Republican voted yes.
The Senate received the bill on June 28, 2019, and referred it to the Committee on Rules and Administration, where no further action was taken before the 116th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Voting machine manufacturers, whose proprietary source code and hardware designs remain undisclosed and whose machines may still connect to networks; the country went into 2020 and 2024 elections with no federal paper-ballot mandate, no required post-election audits, and no internet ban. State election offices that wanted to modernize got no federal grant money for it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Voting machine vendors kept their closed systems

for.name: Zoe Lofgren
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-CA); Chair, House Administration Committee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and reported it out of the House Administration Committee on a 6-3 vote.

for.name: 224 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted unanimously for passage, supplying all but one of the 225 votes in favor.

against.name: 184 of 197 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted against passage, nearly unanimously, after backing a motion to recommit that failed.

against.name: Rodney Davis
against.role: U.S. Representative (R-IL); Ranking Member, House Administration Committee
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to add a requirement that chief state election officials disclose foreign nationals with access to ballots or voting machines; the motion failed 189-220.

against.name: Senate Rules and Administration Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on June 28, 2019, and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the SAFE Act or companion election security bills to the Senate floor in 2019, calling such measures unnecessary; the bill died without a Senate vote.

sides.party_line_note: Passage split almost perfectly by party: 224 of 234 voting Democrats voted yes and 184 of 198 voting Republicans voted no, with one Republican in favor and six Democrats against on the failed motion to recommit.

industries.industry: Election technology and voting machine vendors
industries.note: The bill would have forced vendors to publish source code and hardware designs under royalty-free licenses, build machines in the United States, report cyber incidents within three days, and decertify noncompliant systems — dismantling the proprietary, closed-system business model. The public's interest in verifiable elections ran directly against the industry's interest in secrecy.

industries.industry: Cybersecurity services and election infrastructure vendors
industries.note: The bill funded states to buy security assessments, cyber training, and technical support from qualified vendors, though only U.S.-owned vendors meeting disclosure criteria qualified.
A federal mandate for individual paper ballots in every federal election, printed in the U.S. on recycled American paper, would have created large recurring demand for ballot stock and printing.
